newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX opens new facility amid cheers and gripes.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX opens new facility amid cheers and gripes.

text.p: A mixture of cheers and gripes were heard from dealers at the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) on Monday amid a ribbon cutting ceremony for the first trading day in the exchange's new facility.
"I feel like I am at a Yankee-Met game," New York City Mayor Rudolph Guiliani told the rambunctious crowd before the ribbon was cut.
"This is the side of the river you belong on," Guiliani added. NYMEX, which bills itself as the world's largest energy and precious metals exchange in the world, had considered moving to New Jersey.
Generous tax breaks and $128 million in cash from the city and state convinced NYMEX to stay and build a facility at the World Financial Center in downtown New York.

But, technical problems that delayed the move to the new $228 million 16-story building have not been totally resolved. Several dealers complained about difficulties with their state-of-the-art phones, a lifeline for dealmaking.
"One guy was talking and suddenly he found himself in a three way conversation with another guy who happened to call in on another line," said a floor trader of crude oil who requested anonymity.

Traders of gold voiced particular frustration as their phone problems coincided with a sharp fall in gold prices on opening day. Still, dealers said it was unclear whether the new phones actually had problems or whether traders still needed to learn how to use them.

The two cavernous 25,000 square foot trading floors - one for the energy exchange and one for the metals exchange - effectively quadruples the size of the old exchange which is just several blocks away.
Dealers complain that the price boards are harder to see since they are farther away and the warehouse-like acoustics make it harder to hear. But, most say it is just a matter of adjustment.
"Everything is ready to go. We don't see any problems. The rest is just a matter of adjustment," said Howard Hopkins, crude trader with Merrill Lynch.
But, NYMEX conceded that some direct lines from outside offices to the floor were not working, but speed dial functions were able to circumvent the problem.

"There are a couple of direct lines that will be up by tomorrow. The bottom line is that any issue there is will not interrupt business and will be resolved by tomorrow morning," said Nachamah Jacobovitz, spokeswoman for NYMEX.
Happiest with the move seemed to be city officials who saved 8,100 jobs and gained $2 billion in revenue that city officials said NYMEX will generate annually for New York.

"Although it generates a lot of money and jobs, the bottom line was that we had to keep it here since it is vitally important for us to remain a world financial center," said New York City councilwoman Kathryn Freed.
